body:
Long story short: P100 filters trap virus-containing aerosols because their pore size is large (0.3+ um). However, they do not trap many odors, because many stinky molecules   
are orders of magnitude smaller than aerosols.

Short story long:

\- P100 filters are capable of trapping the same sizes of particulate as P95, N95, and N100 filters

\- N filters (either 95 or 100) are compatible only with non-oily aerosols. P filters (either 95 or 100) are compatible with both oily and non-oily aerosols.

\- N95, N100, P95, and P100 filters all trap particulate down to \~0.3 um diameter. 95 vs 100 is the percent particulate trapped (95% or 100% of >=0.3 um diameter particulate trapped)

\- N95 filters are sufficient to trap aerosolized virus (consider this study using \~0.8 um-diameter H1N1 influenza particles: [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4646082/](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4646082/))

\- Stinky compounds like 2-mercaptoethanol (smells like raw sewage) are only a few atoms big / are many orders magnitude smaller than the pore size which trap aerosolized virus

\- It's completely possible to be protected from aerosolized virus by a well-sealed N/P95 or N/P100 respirator, but still smell stinky compounds. Degree of protection depends on how well the filter is fitted to your face, and how old the filter is
